summary: Describes how GMPLS can control two types of Ethernet switching defined for Metro Ethernet Forum and ITU G.8011 services. It specifies how GMPLS is used to set up such Ethernet services across the network.

plainLanguage.summary: Companies buy Ethernet services that act like private wires between sites. This explains how a single control system can set up those wires on the network switches.

questions: gmpls support for metro ethernet forum services

subtitle: How GMPLS signaling sets up Ethernet private line and virtual private line connections for Metro Ethernet Forum and ITU G.8011 services.

tldr.problem: Metro Ethernet Forum (MEF) and ITU G.8011 define Ethernet services such as private lines, but say nothing about the switching technology under them or how to control it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses GMPLS signaling with Call procedures and adds an Endpoint ID TLV, an L2CP TLV, a Line LSP encoding type and an EVPL switching type with a VLAN ID label, so that EPL and EVPL connections can be signaled.
tldr.outcome: It covers point-to-point service only, and is aimed at the network control needed for MEF UNI Type 3. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6004 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2010. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Ethernet Services and GMPLS
sections.content:
The Metro Ethernet Forum (MEF 6) and ITU-T G.8011 describe Ethernet services in transport networks from the point of view of the service, not the technology underneath. Within that framework, G.8011.1 defines the Ethernet Private Line (EPL) service and G.8011.2 defines the Ethernet Virtual Private Line (EVPL) service. MEF 6 covers both.

This document defines the GMPLS extensions to control the kinds of switching that support those services. It does not define the UNI or External NNI reference points (see RFC 6005 for the UNI). It builds on RFC 3473, the Call procedures of RFC 4974, the generic extensions in RFC 6002 and the traffic parameters of RFC 6003.
sections.plainLanguage: Ethernet services describe what customers get, like a private wire. This RFC describes how the network's control system builds that wire.

sections.title: Scope and Signaled Attributes
sections.content:
MEF and G.8011 define point-to-point (P2P) and multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) connectivity. This document supports P2P, which corresponds clearly to GMPLS P2P TE LSPs. MP2MP service, which MEF calls E-LAN, is left for future study.

MEF 11 defines UNI types. In Type 1, services are configured manually. In Type 2 they may be configured manually or through a link management interface. In Type 3 they may be established through a signaling interface. This document, together with RFC 6005, is aimed at the network control needed for Type 3.

Attributes tied to the local physical connection are static and are left out of signaling. The attributes that are signaled are endpoint identifiers, connection identifiers, traffic parameters, the bundling and VLAN ID map (EVPL only) and VLAN ID preservation (EVPL only).
sections.plainLanguage: Some settings never change, like which plug a wire is in. Only the settings that differ for each connection need to be sent.

sections.title: Common Signaling Support
sections.content:
Procedures for RSVP objects are unchanged except where this document says otherwise. Ethernet endpoint identifiers are character based, while GMPLS identifiers are normally IP addresses. To bridge this, the RFC borrows the Call mechanism of RFC 4974. The Ethernet connection identifier is treated as the long Call ID, and the endpoint identifier travels in a new Endpoint ID TLV inside the CALL_ATTRIBUTES object. When a Call is set up or torn down, a CALL_ATTRIBUTES object with an Endpoint ID TLV MUST be included in the Notify message along with the long Call ID.

A Call is only established when LSPs are needed. The initiator MUST first establish a Call, then at least one Ethernet LSP SHOULD follow. When the last LSP of a Call is removed, the Call SHOULD be torn down. Nodes MUST support both network-initiated and user-initiated Calls.
sections.plainLanguage: Network gear likes numeric addresses, but customers name their ends with words. The RFC adds a label-holder that carries the word-name alongside the usual numbers.

sections.title: Traffic Parameters and L2CP
sections.content:
Service attributes are carried in the FLOWSPEC and TSPEC objects using RFC 6003 traffic parameters: bandwidth profile, VLAN Class of Service preservation and Layer 2 Control Protocol (L2CP) processing. The Switching Granularity field of the Ethernet SENDER_TSPEC MUST be set to zero.

Because RFC 6003 does not define L2CP attributes but allows them in a TLV, this RFC defines the L2CP TLV. Its Type MUST be 3 and its Length MUST be 8. It holds a 4-bit Ingress L2CP (IL2CP) field, a 4-bit Egress L2CP (EL2CP) field and 24 reserved bits that MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt. Ethernet connections established under this document MUST include the L2CP TLV. When MEF services are used, EL2CP MUST be 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides speed, a connection needs rules for what to do with the network's own chatter messages. A small field says whether to block, process or pass them along.

sections.title: EPL Service Signaling
sections.content:
EPL carries Ethernet over dedicated bandwidth, point-to-point connections. G.8011.1 defines two types: type 1 works at the MAC frame layer and type 2 at the line encoding layer, for example 8B/10B. MEF 6 defines only one EPL type, matching type 1.

The two types differ only in the LSP Encoding Type: Ethernet (2) for type 1 and MEF, and Line (14) for type 2. Both use Switching Type DCSC (125) and G-PID Ethernet PHY (33). These parameters MUST be used, together with the common procedures and the RFC 3473 procedures for bidirectional LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: An EPL is a whole wire reserved for one customer. Two flavors exist, depending on how closely the wire's signal is read.

sections.title: EVPL Service Signaling
sections.content:
EVPL allows multiple Ethernet connections per port, each supporting a specific set of VLAN IDs. LSPs for EVPL MUST use Switching Type EVPL (30), LSP Encoding Type Ethernet (2) and G-PID Ethernet PHY (33), plus the EVPL Generalized Label and the Generalized Channel_Set Label objects from RFC 6002.

The EVPL Generalized Label (Label Type 2) is 16 bits: 4 reserved bits that MUST be zero and ignored on receipt, then a 12-bit VLAN ID.

Unless the explicit label control mechanism of RFC 3473 and RFC 4003 is used to request VLAN ID mapping, VLAN IDs MUST be preserved across an LSP. Mapping applies when the service is not configured for both bundling and VLAN ID preservation.

A single LSP SHOULD be used per EVPL connection when its Path and Resv messages fit in one unfragmented IP packet, and Channel_Set changes use make-before-break. Bundling many VLAN IDs can make a Path message too large, so multiple LSPs MAY be used within the same Call. They share objects except the SENDER_TEMPLATE, SESSION and label-related objects, and SHOULD share resources. Adding VLAN IDs can use a new LSP or make-before-break. Changing other service parameters requires re-signaling all LSPs of the Call via make-before-break.
sections.plainLanguage: An EVPL is one shared wire that carries several separate networks, each marked with a tag number. If the list of tags gets too long for one message, the connection can be split across several messages.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA made three assignments. The Endpoint ID TLV was added to the Call Attributes TLV registry as type 2. The Line (e.g., 8B/10B) LSP Encoding Type was assigned value 14. The Ethernet Virtual Private Line (EVPL) switching type was assigned value 30, which is also reflected in IANAGmplsSwitchingTypeTC of the IANA-GMPLS-TC-MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: New names were added to the official lists of numbers so every vendor uses the same ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC introduces new message object formats for GMPLS signaling but no new signaling messages, and does not change the relationship between adjacent Label Switching Routers in the control plane. It therefore adds no security considerations beyond those in RFC 3473.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is added to who talks to whom, so the old safety rules still apply.
